title: How Massive Is Elon Musk’s Trillion-Dollar Fortune? Spend It Yourself
gist: WIRED and Neal Agarwal launched 'Spend Elon Musk's Money,' a 3D visualization of a roughly $1 trillion fortune tied up mostly in SpaceX and Tesla shares. In an interview, Agarwal discusses the web as a medium, viral emergent behavior, the technical limits of rendering millions of objects, and price inflation visible since his Bill Gates version.

themes.theme: Musk's wealth and the trillionaire scale

insights.claim: Elon Musk is worth about a trillion dollars on any given day, mostly in SpaceX and Tesla shares rather than cash, with Neuralink and Boring Company additional.
insights.speaker: Brian Barrett
insights.so_what: Musk's net worth is concentrated in two equities, so it tracks them.
insights.locator: On any given day, Elon Musk is worth

insights.claim: Humans struggle to grasp large numbers, so 'trillion' sounds like a short hop from 'billion' despite being 1,000 times larger; interactive spending visualizations make it tangible.
insights.speaker: Brian Barrett
insights.so_what: Framing wealth in tangible terms shapes public perception of inequality.
insights.locator: “Trillionaire” is an easy enough word to say

insights.claim: Spend Elon Musk's Money is a 3D sequel to Spend Bill Gates' Money, where players buy items from Big Macs to aircraft carriers and the Las Vegas Sphere and see them in physical space.
insights.speaker: Brian Barrett
insights.so_what: Shows how media makers are packaging wealth concentration as interactive content.
insights.locator: WIRED has partnered with Neal Agarwal

insights.claim: Agarwal says the original Gates version launched with his site, showcased $100 billion, and kept finding new audiences, and that the trillion scale prompted a 3D redo.
insights.speaker: Neal Agarwal
insights.so_what: Evidence of enduring audience appetite for wealth visualizations.
insights.quote: The game kept finding a new audience over and over again
insights.locator: It was one of the biggest things I’ve launched

insights.claim: Agarwal says the infinite space of the web lets you visualize huge numbers in ways physical media cannot, such as The Deep Sea, which would be a mile long if printed.
insights.speaker: Neal Agarwal
insights.so_what: Argues for the web's unique advantages as a medium.
insights.locator: I think that’s one thing the web is actually really good at

insights.claim: Rendering a million monster trucks as 3D models would freeze a laptop, so Agarwal used tricks to get the 3D effect without actual models.
insights.speaker: Neal Agarwal
insights.so_what: Browser rendering limits constrain large-scale 3D visualization.
insights.locator: Initially I wanted everything to be 3D models

themes.theme: Web as a medium and emergent behavior

insights.claim: Viral projects produce unexpected user behavior: Infinite Craft players crafted enough Japanese words to play entirely in Japanese, and Internet Road Trip players formed a Discord and began birdwatching.
insights.speaker: Neal Agarwal
insights.so_what: Open web experiences can spawn communities that creators do not plan.
insights.locator: I think each project has been very different

insights.claim: Agarwal prefers the open web to apps because Apple and Google approval can take a week and offer no recourse, whereas a homepage lets him publish whatever he wants.
insights.speaker: Neal Agarwal
insights.so_what: App store gatekeeping pushes some creators back to the open web.
insights.quote: Nobody can tell me what to do with it.
insights.locator: When I was a teenager I did make some apps

insights.claim: A Big Mac in the original Gates version cost $2 and costs $6 now in the Musk version, which Agarwal calls very inflation-adjusted given only six or seven years.
insights.speaker: Neal Agarwal
insights.so_what: Anecdotal evidence of food-price inflation over roughly six to seven years.
insights.locator: It doesn’t just tell us about Elon Musk
